beats.text: A patient arrives in the emergency department, lying on a stretcher, with a wound on the abdomen.
One doctor writes that the wound is above the navel. But above means what? Closer to the ceiling... or closer to the head?
If every clinician described the body from their own point of view, nobody would agree on anything.
Anatomy solves this with a shared language: one fixed reference position, a set of imaginary planes, and precise terms for direction and movement.
By the end of this lecture, you'll speak that language fluently.
Introduction to Anatomy.
Here's what you'll be able to do. Define the standard anatomical position.
Describe the anatomical planes, and the body sections they create.
Identify the major terms of position and direction.
Describe the basic movements, using the correct terminology.
And apply all of it to simple clinical and anatomical examples.
First, the word itself. Anatomy comes from Greek roots meaning cutting up. In other words, dissection.
That's how anatomy began: by carefully opening the body, to see how it is built.
Structures you can study with the naked eye, like bones, muscles, and organs such as the heart, belong to gross, or macroscopic, anatomy.
Zoom in further, past the limit of the eye, and you need a microscope. That's microscopic anatomy.
It includes histology, the study of tissues...
and cytology, the study of cells.
In this lecture, we stay at the gross level.
Here's our route.
We'll begin with the anatomical position.
Then cut the body with three planes.
Learn the terms of direction.
Put the body in motion.
And finish with a clinical case, and a quick self-test.
Every anatomical description assumes the body is in one standard posture: the anatomical position.
Let's build it. First, the body stands upright.
The feet are together and flat, with the toes pointing forward.
The upper limbs hang at the sides.
And here's the detail students most often forget: the palms face forward, with the fingers straight and together.
This is the anatomical position. Seen from the front, the anterior view... and from the back, the posterior view.
Here's the key rule. Whether the patient is lying down, sitting, or turned away from you, we describe structures as if the body were in this position.
It is the standard reference for everything that follows.
Now imagine slicing through the body with flat, imaginary sheets. These are the anatomical planes, and three major planes are commonly used.
The first is the coronal plane, also called the frontal plane. It is oriented vertically, passing from one side of the body to the other.
Watch what it does. It divides the body into an anterior part, in front...
and a posterior part, behind.
The second is the sagittal plane. It is also oriented vertically, but turned ninety degrees, running from front to back.
A sagittal plane divides the body into right and left parts.
There are many possible sagittal planes. Away from the center, the two parts are unequal.
But one is special. The midsagittal plane passes through the center of the body...
dividing it into equal right and left halves.
The third plane is the transverse plane, also called the horizontal, or axial, plane.
Unlike the other two, it runs horizontally, parallel to the ground.
It divides the body into a superior part, above, and an inferior part, below.
So, three planes.
Coronal: anterior and posterior.
Sagittal: right and left.
Transverse: superior and inferior.
With the body positioned and divided, we can describe where things are. Three major pairs of terms locate structures relative to the body as a whole, or to other structures.
Anterior, or ventral, means toward the front of the body.
Posterior, or dorsal, means toward the back of the body.
Medial means closer to the body's midline. Lateral means farther from it.
The nose is medial to the eyes. The arms are lateral to the chest.
And right and left always mean the patient's right and left, not yours.
Superior means above another structure, or toward the head.
Inferior means below another structure, or toward the feet.
For example, the head is superior to the shoulders.
Notice that each term is a comparison. A structure is never simply medial. It is medial to something.
Some terms are built for the limbs.
Proximal means nearer to the point of attachment to the trunk.
Distal means farther from it.
Follow the upper limb outward: shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand. Each point is distal to the one before it.
So the hand is distal to the elbow... and the elbow is proximal to the hand.
Remember, proximal and distal are commonly used for the limbs.
Along the long axis of the body, two more terms appear. Cranial means toward the head, the same idea as superior.
Caudal means toward the feet, matching inferior.
Finally, depth.
Superficial means closer to the surface of the body. Deep means farther from the surface.
Let's move through the face, layer by layer.
On the surface, the skin.
Beneath it, subcutaneous fat.
Then the SMAS fascia layer...
the facial muscles...
and the neurovascular layer.
And deepest of all, the skull.
So, the skin is superficial to the bones.
And inside the skull lies the brain. The brain is deep to the skull.
Now let's put the body in motion. Movement terms describe what happens at joints, and most of them come in opposing pairs.
Watch the elbow.
As the forearm bends up toward the arm, the angle between the two bones gets smaller.
That's flexion: a movement that decreases the angle between two bones, and typically produces bending.
Now reverse it. The angle opens, and the joint straightens.
That's extension: a movement that increases the angle between two bones.
For the next pair, the midline becomes our reference. Start in the anatomical position.
Raise the arm out to the side, away from the midline.
This is abduction: moving a limb away from the midline.
Bring it back down, toward the body.
This is adduction: moving a limb toward the midline.
A simple memory trick: in adduction, you add the limb back to the body.
Combine these movements in sequence, and something new appears.
Flexion, forward.
Abduction, out to the side.
Extension, backward.
Adduction, back toward the midline.
Performed continuously, the hand traces a circle, and the limb sweeps out a cone.
This is circumduction: a sequential combination of flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction.
Rotation is movement around a long axis. To see it clearly, bend the elbow to ninety degrees, so the forearm points forward, like a pointer.
The axis runs straight down the length of the arm.
Now turn the arm, so the forearm swings across the body. The anterior surface moves toward the midline.
That's medial rotation.
Turn it the other way, and the anterior surface moves away from the midline.
That's lateral rotation.
The axis itself doesn't move. The limb turns around it.
The forearm has its own special rotation. Start in the anatomical position, with the palm facing forward.
Here, the two forearm bones, the radius and the ulna, lie parallel. This is supination.
Now turn the palm to face backward. The radius rotates over the ulna, and the two bones cross.
This is pronation: it turns the palm posteriorly.
Turn it back, and the palm faces anteriorly again.
That's supination: it turns the palm anteriorly.
Notice: the anatomical position is a supinated position.
Some movements are simple glides, forward and backward, up and down.
Move the jaw forwards. That's protraction.
Move the jaw backwards. That's retraction.
Elevation moves a body part upward, superiorly. Raising the shoulders is elevation.
So is raising the mandible, when you close the mouth.
Depression moves a body part downward, inferiorly. Lowering the shoulders after raising them is depression.
So is lowering the mandible, when you open the mouth.
The foot has movements of its own.
Move the dorsum of the foot, the top surface, upwards. That's dorsiflexion.
Move the foot downward, pointing the toes. That's plantar flexion.
Now look at the feet from the front, and watch the soles.
Turning the sole toward the midline is inversion.
Turning the sole away from the midline is eversion.
Let's apply this. A twenty-two-year-old football player twists his right ankle during a match.
On examination, the physician asks him to turn the sole of his foot outward, away from the midline, to assess the integrity of the lateral ankle structures.
Which anatomical term describes this movement? Inversion, eversion, dorsiflexion, or plantar flexion? Pause, and decide.
The answer is eversion. The sole turns away from the midline.
Inversion would turn the sole toward the midline. And dorsiflexion and plantar flexion move the foot up and down, not side to side.
Now, a quick self-test. Answer each one before the reveal.
Which plane divides the body into superior and inferior parts?
The transverse plane.
This arm is moving toward the midline. Name the movement.
Adduction.
Is the hand proximal, or distal, to the elbow?
Distal.
The palm turns to face backward. What is this movement?
Pronation.
Let's bring it all together.
The anatomical position provides the standard reference for describing structures.
Coronal, sagittal, and transverse planes describe body sections.
Directional terms describe the relative location of structures.
Movement terms describe common joint and body movements.
Together, these terms provide a common language for anatomical and clinical communication. Learn them well. You'll use them every single day.
For further reading, see Gray's Anatomy for Students, and Last's Anatomy.
